title: The List
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 24 of 40
content:
Danse knew something was wrong before anyone told him.

That was the cruelty of being observant.

Quinlan stopped meeting his eyes.

Kells requested reports he had already received.

Maxson cancelled a briefing without explanation.

Haylen found reasons to be elsewhere whenever Danse entered the room.

He noticed every piece.

For two days he said nothing.

On the third night he found me near the Prydwen’s aft storage section.

“Walk with me.”

Not a request.

I followed.

He led me to an empty maintenance corridor and stopped.

“Has anyone spoken to you about me?”

My stomach tightened.

“No.”

“That was too fast.”

“It was true.”

Danse studied my face.

“Something’s happening.”

“I noticed.”

“What?”

“I don’t know.”

He turned away.

“Quinlan’s Institute data.”

“What about it?”

“He decoded part of an escapee registry.”

The words sounded ordinary.

His expression did not.

“I asked to see it. He refused.”

“That doesn’t mean it’s about you.”

“No.”

“But you think it is.”

Danse looked at me.

“I think people I trust are behaving like they know something I don’t.”

Fear looked strange on him.

Not because he was never afraid.

Because he usually converted fear into action before anyone could see it.

Now there was no target.

I reached for his hand.

He let me take it.

“Whatever it is, we handle it.”

“You don’t know that.”

“No.”

He looked down at our fingers.

“You say that a lot.”

“What?”

“That you don’t know.”

“Reality refuses to brief me in advance.”

His mouth moved faintly.

Then boots sounded at the end of the corridor.

Haylen appeared.

She stopped when she saw us holding hands.

Usually she would have smiled.

This time she looked like she might cry.

Danse released me.

“Scribe.”

“Paladin.”

He stared at her.

“Tell me.”

Haylen’s face went pale.

“I can’t.”

“That confirms there’s something to tell.”

“Danse—”

“Is my command in question?”

“No.”

“My loyalty?”

She looked away.

Danse flinched as if struck.

“Haylen.”

“I’m sorry.”

She left before he could stop her.

Danse stood motionless.

I touched his arm.

He pulled away.

Not from me.

From everything.

“I need to speak with Quinlan.”

“Let me come.”

“No.”

“Danse.”

“This is Brotherhood business.”

“So am I, apparently.”

His expression hardened.

“Not this.”

Then he walked away.

He did not return that night.

Or the next morning.

By afternoon, his bunk was untouched.

His power armor station was empty.

The Prydwen felt wrong without him.

Nobody would answer me.

Rhys looked genuinely frightened when I asked.

Kells ordered me to stand down.

Quinlan would only say, “The matter is under review.”

I considered throwing him over the rail.

Haylen found me first.

She pulled me into the same maintenance corridor where Danse had questioned me.

Her hands were shaking.

“He’s gone.”

“I know.”

“No. I mean gone. He left the Prydwen.”

“Where?”

“I don’t know.”

“You know something else.”

Haylen closed her eyes.

“The Institute list included a synth designation. M7-97.”

My blood went cold.

She continued because stopping would have been worse.

“The DNA profile matched Danse.”

For a moment the airship vanished.

There was only the sound of Danse saying I’m not a machine on the road outside ArcJet.

Nick Valentine beneath Diamond City lights.

Amos in his greenhouse.

Cutler changing beneath his skin.

Danse’s absolute belief that categories were truth.

“No,” I said.

Haylen’s face broke.

“I checked it three times.”

“That doesn’t mean—”

“I know.”

“Does Maxson know?”

“Yes.”

“What’s the order?”

She looked at me.

I knew before she spoke.

“Execution.”

The word turned the corridor into ice.

I pushed past her.

Haylen caught my arm.

“Wait.”

“For what?”

“Maxson is looking for you.”

“Good.”

“No. Listen to me.”

Her grip tightened.

“Danse has a fallback location. Listening Post Bravo. He used it in case Cambridge was compromised.”

I stared at her.

“You’re telling me where he is.”

“I’m telling you where he might be.”

“Why?”

Tears stood in her eyes.

“Because he saved my life more times than I can count.”

I thought of Danse calling attachment dangerous.

Too late.

It had already happened to all of us.

I squeezed Haylen’s hand once.

Then I went to find Maxson.

Maxson was not in his command quarters when I found him.

Kells was.

The captain took one look at my face and shut the door behind me.

“You have been ordered to stand by.”

“Where is Danse?”

“That information is restricted.”

“So you know.”

Kells’ expression did not change.

“Paladin Danse is the subject of a security investigation.”

“His name is on an Institute escape list.”

That made him pause.

Haylen’s disclosure had crossed a line. I knew it. So did he.

Kells folded his hands behind his back.

“You should leave this alone.”

“Can you?”

His eyes sharpened.

“This is not about me.”

“It’s about a man you served with.”

“It is about a synth infiltrating the Brotherhood.”

The phrasing was already changing him.

Not Danse.

A synth.

An infiltrator.

I felt sick.

“Did Quinlan find evidence he was sending information to the Institute?”

“No.”

“Sabotage?”

“No.”

“Hidden orders?”

“Unknown.”

“So the only thing that changed is what you learned he is.”

Kells’ mouth tightened.

“That alone is sufficient.”

For the Brotherhood, maybe it was.

That was the horror.

I left before the argument became useless.

Haylen met me near the lower gantry. Rhys stood with her.

That surprised me more than anything that day.

He looked furious.

Not at me.

At the deck.

“Rhys?”

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to.”

Haylen touched his arm.

Rhys pulled away and paced two steps.

“He’s an asshole,” he said.

I stared.

“Danse?”

“Maxson.”

Haylen closed her eyes.

Rhys kept going.

“Danse dragged me out of Cambridge after Keane went down. Carried me in power armor for three miles because I couldn’t put weight on my leg.”

His voice became rough.

“He sat with Worwick when he was dying. He wrote every family notification himself even though half of us didn’t have families left to notify.”

Rhys swallowed hard.

“And now I’m supposed to believe none of that counts because some Institute file has a number on it?”

I had never liked him more.

“Do you?” I asked.

He looked at me as if I had insulted him.

“I don’t know what I believe.”

Honest.

Painfully so.

Haylen rubbed at her eyes.

“We can’t all leave. If we do, they’ll know.”

“Know what?” Rhys asked.

“That we’re helping.”

He looked toward the command deck.

Then at me.

“What do you need?”

The question almost undid me.

“Time.”

Rhys nodded.

“I can create a maintenance fault in the flight schedule.”

Haylen stared at him.

“You can?”

“No.”

He looked offended.

“But Lancer-Captain Kells thinks I’m an idiot, so if I break something by accident nobody will be surprised.”

Despite everything, I laughed.

Haylen did too, once, wetly.

For one moment we were back in Cambridge and Danse was about to tell all of us to act professionally.

The absence of his voice hurt.

Rhys’ expression changed.

“Find him.”

“I will.”

“And if he…”

He could not finish.

I understood.

“If I can bring him back, I will.”

Not to the Brotherhood.

To himself.

Rhys nodded.

Haylen pressed the access code for Bravo into my palm.

Rhys swore under his breath.

Haylen immediately started checking the corridor as if Maxson might personally emerge from a maintenance hatch.

“Listen,” she said. “Danse won’t run because he thinks he deserves whatever happens.”

“I know.”

“He’ll call it duty.”

“I know.”

“He’ll make it sound reasonable.”

That frightened me because she was right.

Rhys leaned against the bulkhead, arms crossed so tightly his knuckles had gone pale.

“For what it’s worth,” he said, “I thought he was an asshole when I met him.”

Haylen stared at him.

“What?”

“You still think he’s an asshole.”

“Yeah, but he’s *our* asshole.”

The laugh escaped me before I could stop it.

Haylen covered her mouth.

Rhys looked offended. “I’m trying to be supportive.”

“You’re doing great.”

His expression crumpled for half a second.

“Just bring him back.”

There were no jokes left after that.

Haylen pulled me into a brief, fierce hug before I could react.

She stepped back immediately, wiping at her face with the heel of her hand.

“If he says he deserves it, don’t believe him.”

“I won’t.”

“He’ll sound convincing.”

“I know.”

Rhys looked toward the ceiling speakers. “Maxson’s going to notice if you don’t go.”

“I know.”

Nobody moved.

The Prydwen hummed around us, enormous and familiar to them, suddenly hostile in a way the metal had not changed enough to explain.

The ship was the same.

The category attached to Danse was different.

Apparently that was all it took.

Then the shipwide speakers called my designation to Maxson’s command deck.

The three of us looked at one another.

“Guess he’s ready,” I said.

Haylen gripped my hand.

“Don’t let him make you forget who Danse is.”

I closed my fingers around the code.

“That’s the one thing I’m sure of.”

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
